newsitem.title: USA: Smith & Wesson sets sights on children's market.
newsitem.headline: Smith & Wesson sets sights on children's market.

text.p: The largest handgun maker in the United States has set its sights on expanding its market to families and children.

Springfield, Massachusetts-based Smith & Wesson, owned by Tomkins Ltd of England, has opened a $3 million National Firearms Training Center that looks more like a suburban shopping mall than a firing range.

Company officials said the facility, which offers weapons, ammunition and apparel as well as training, is an effort to build a wider market for its firearms at a time of growing public concern about handgun use. It is also a move to appeal to the mainstream in a business that is politically polarized.

"With any company, there is always an issue with what you do with the next generation," Smith & Wesson spokesman Ken Jorgensen said. "You overcome a lot of myths when you pick up a gun, with the right supervision, and begin shooting. We're seeing families coming in, and couples."

If the firearms training center proves a success, he said, Smith & Wesson may open similar ones elsewhere. The center is open to anyone who signs up, pays $35 and sits through an hour-long orientation. After a quick course, they are able to squeeze off a few clips under a range officer's supervision.

In its first two weeks, children and families were among those going through orientations and prowling the retail store. Boy Scout leader John Rattelsdorfer of West Springfield visited with a group of scouts in tow, including his son.

The boy's mother, Loretta, said later she was not sure she wanted her son to continue exploring his interest in firearms, including the family's old Civil War-era pistol. "He's interested in guns, but he's young," she said.

Instructor Kenneth Tingley said he has been keeping an eye on the children who have sat through the mandatory orientations to make sure they are absorbing the material. Some have been as young as seven years old.

Instructor Judy Woolley said some of the parents signing their children up to shoot are people who own firearms and want to pass along a family tradition. Others, though, say they know little about shooting and simply want to make sure their children understand gun safety, should they come upon a weapon.
"So they understand the power they have in their hands," Woolley said.
